question: Let a geometric progression with \(n\) terms have first term one, common ratio \(r\) and sum \(s,\) where \(r\) and \(s\) are not zero. The sum of the geometric progression formed by replacing each term of the original progression by its reciprocal is
solution:
The original terms are \(1,r,r^2,\ldots,r^{n-1}\). Multiplying their reciprocals by the last original term produces these same powers in reverse order.

For \(n=1\), both sums equal \(1\), and the proposed expression \(s/r^{n-1}\) also equals \(1\). For \(n\ge2\), let \(T\) be the reciprocal sum. Distributing \(r^{n-1}\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
r^{n-1}T
&=r^{n-1}\left(1+\frac1r+\cdots+\frac1{r^{n-1}}\right)\\
&=r^{n-1}+r^{n-2}+\cdots+r+1\\
&=s.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each original term appears exactly once, so reversing the order does not change the sum. Since \(r\ne0\), we may divide by \(r^{n-1}\), obtaining
\[
T=\boxed{\frac{s}{r^{n-1}}}.
\]
This argument also applies when \(r=1\) or when \(r\) is negative. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
Taking reciprocals changes the common ratio from \(r\) to \(1/r\). We can therefore compare the finite geometric-sum formulas for these two ratios. Let \(T\) denote the reciprocal sum.

If \(r=1\), every term in both progressions is \(1\). Thus \(s=T=n\), giving \(T=s/r^{n-1}\).

If \(r\ne1\), the original sum is
\[
s=\frac{r^n-1}{r-1}.
\]
The reciprocal progression has first term \(1\) and common ratio \(1/r\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
T
&=\frac{(1/r)^n-1}{(1/r)-1}\\
&=\frac{(1-r^n)/r^n}{(1-r)/r}\\
&=\frac{r^n-1}{r^{n-1}(r-1)}\\
&=\frac{s}{r^{n-1}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
All divisions are valid because this case has \(r\ne0,1\). The calculation includes \(n=1\) and negative ratios as well. Therefore the answer is \(\boxed{\dfrac{s}{r^{n-1}}}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Compare the two geometric-sum formulas
